## Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Martial Arts and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" **·** Socrates, Plato, Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Buddhism; Stoicism; Utilitarianism — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- ch. 6 "Enter the Dragon - Traditional Asian Martial Arts" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Free Your Mind, and Your Roundhouse Will Follow" **·** Aristotle, Confucius, The Buddha — Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Li (ritual propriety); Virtue Ethics (arete); Zen Buddhism — Young argues that dojo courtesy is not the fantasy that good manners win fights (Napoleon and the Karate Kid's Johnny lost on skill, not rudeness) but the framing of a craft within a way of life. He maps Aristotle's techne/ethos distinction onto the Japanese jutsu/do pairing to show founders like Kano, Funakoshi and Ueshiba treated fighting as one part of a whole ethical character, reads his seiza apology to an injured yellow belt through Confucian ren, li, yi and shu, and traces Shinto purity into the sincerity (kime) of committed sparring. His black-belt humiliation by seniors becomes Zen's 'courtesy of brutal': ego-deflating violence that trains no-mindedness (muga, Takuan Soho's fudoshin).
- ch. 8 "2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma" **·** The Buddha — Zen Buddhism; Non-Self (anatman); Emptiness (sunyata); Compassion (karuna) — Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'
- ch. 9 "A Koan" **·** Zen Buddhism — Finnigan and Tanaka use the kendo student Kenzo, struck down whenever he thinks 'Now is the time to strike!', to pose the puzzle of intentional action without thought. They set Donald Davidson's causal theory of action (intentions as belief-desire causes) against Takuan Soho's mushin, which warns that wherever you put your mind it stops, then resolve it: training lets a master act 'as Yagyu would', and giving reasons afterwards is how one accepts responsibility for an action no reason was 'in mind' for. The koan dissolves once how-questions (how could I act without thinking?) are distinguished from why-questions (why did you do that?).
- ch. 10 "And the Winner Is" **·** Plato, The Buddha — Tripartite Soul; Non-Self (anatman); The Philosopher King; Zen Buddhism — Lynch pits Plato against the Shaolin monks on the nature of the self that martial training is supposed to master. Plato's Republic makes the athlete-warrior Guardian a harmonious, rationally ruled tripartite soul whose bravery is 'remembering what ought and ought not to be feared', trained so reason governs aggression; Buddhism instead dissolves the self into five impermanent aggregates (illustrated by the chariot analogy) and reads mushin as a direct taste of no-self. He awards the practical decision to the Buddhist fighting monks, since no-self explains martial spontaneity and naturally arising compassion, while admitting Plato's substantive rational soul is not strictly refuted.
- ch. 11 "Knowledge and Mastery" *(no index entry yet)* — Schubert asks what his own master's certificate actually certified and dismantles two accounts of martial mastery: the 'Secret Knowledge' account (hidden teachings like Crouching Tiger's stolen Wu Dan manual) and the 'Complete Knowledge' account, which absurdly implies mastery is suspended when a new takedown joins the syllabus or his forgetful Iaido master omits a step of a form. Using the distinction between knowing-that, knowing-how and physical ability (he knew how to jump-spin heel-kick with his foot in a cast), he argues mastery is knowing that and how across the essential techniques, principles and strategies a style could have consisted of, by analogy with fluency in a language. Rank, politics and even the ability to perform are at best signs of mastery, not the thing itself.
- ch. 12 "The Karate Kid - Character and Education" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "An Enemy Lying in Ambush" **·** Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius, Zeno of Citium, Seneca — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control — Fuller reads his teenage collapse while holding shiko dachi at his Eighth Kyu grading as a weakness of will, and argues that karate is Stoic discipline embodied. He explains the dichotomy of control through Epictetus's barbecue etiquette and the Kill Bill II buried-alive scene (only the Bride's years of disciplined training, not magic, break the coffin), then lays out living according to nature, Zeno's apatheia, Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, and Seneca's nightly self-examination as the model of askesis. Kata becomes 'a defiant stand against irrational emotion-chasing', and since only virtue is up to us, the enemy 'lying in ambush' is always internal: ourselves.
- ch. 14 "Don’t Carry the World upon Your Shoulders. Only Your Opponent" **·** Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill — Utilitarianism; The Greatest Happiness Principle; The Hedonic Calculus — Cooper and Taylor argue that Kano's judo principles, seiryokuzenyou (maximum efficiency) and jitakyouei (mutual welfare and benefit), echo Bentham's principle of utility: both men swept away archaic rules to reach one efficient ethical goal, and Kano accepted the comparison. They run the hedonic calculus over training bruises versus the joy of a clean throw, use Mill's secondary principles as rule-utilitarian guidelines (release the armbar at the tap rather than calculating each time), and answer the objection that utilitarianism demands too much with Kano's own ethos: like judo, it is about continual improvement, not impossible maximization.
- ch. 15 "Living the Absurd Life" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Friedrich Nietzsche — Existentialism; Existence Precedes Essence; The Absurd; Authenticity — Krein asks why he has spent fifteen years on karate when pepper spray and avoidance would serve self-defense better, and answers with existentialism rather than Buddhism. Nietzsche's death of God and Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence leave life objectively meaningless, but the dojo supplies a self-contained standard for Sartrean transcendence (kata quality is judged within the art), trains the courage and clarity authenticity requires, and enforces excuse-free responsibility: in sparring you either score or you don't. Studying a traditional martial art is thus a heroic, 'act without hope' defiance of the absurd.
- ch. 16 "The Last Resort" **·** Michel Foucault — Feminism; Power/Knowledge — Petersen recounts fighting off a man who threatened to rape and kill her, and argues that karate, not feminist doctrine or therapy, made her a real feminist by rewiring her self-concept, fear responses and relationships. Against the Lara Croft fantasy she sets practical self-defense doctrine ('don't be there'; assertiveness, not aggression, with the bus pest), Australian, US and UN statistics on violence against women, and the Guthrie study of Chicago's feminist Thousand Waves dojo. She frames the transformation with Foucault's 'care of the self': karate's practices of the self give women power through knowledge, so that by black-belt time enduring harassment simply 'isn't who she is'.
- ch. 17 "The Way of the Place" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete) — Beattie uses Henri Lefebvre's account of the production of space to read the dojo as a 'differential space' practitioners actively create against abstract, conformist space. He shows how bow-ins, founder portraits, Japanese counting, mats, dogi and belt hierarchies mark ownership, bind the school to a lineage, separate 'dojo' from 'street', and shape bodies and safety (with Kendo's door-side seating and MMA's display of physique as hierarchy written into space). Play matters too: Aristotle's point that virtues are built by habit explains how playing at combat in a safe place breeds real courage, and the whole exercise teaches a moving balance between inside and outside.
- ch. 18 "The Perfect Weapon - Ethics and Value" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Back at the Bins, or Loving Your Enemy Like Your Neighbor" **·** Emmanuel Levinas, Hannah Arendt, Immanuel Kant — The Face of the Other; The Categorical Imperative — Kohn begins with her own response to a serial bin-tipper: practicing iaido sword draws in full view of the neighbours to intimidate an imagined Other. Contrasting iaido's virtual opponent (a mere tool for the self) with aikido's real partners, she deploys Levinas's face of the Other, responsibility without waiting for reciprocity and philosophy as 'the Wisdom of Love', alongside Arendt's shared responsibility for the world's conflicts, to argue that care for even one's attacker comes first, with Kant's categorical imperative as the generalizable counterpart to Levinas's ethics. Her confession: she treated the imagined culprit as an object of hate, when meeting 'the Face' would have demanded an apology and maybe a hug.
- ch. 20 "Why It Matters" **·** The Buddha — Russell, who at eleven believed practice would let her kill a bull with one blow, argues that martial arts culture systematically breeds epistemic vices: gullibility (ki knockouts, chocolate milk for recovery), closed-mindedness, dojos treated like churches, sunk-cost defence of the side-kick-knifes-from-hands story, and deference to sensei and founders (Funakoshi curing fevers with karate). She diagnoses data-poverty, since lethal techniques cannot be ethically tested, as the enabling condition, and prescribes cautious belief, closing with the Buddha's counsel from Harry Cook's dojo wall: believe nothing on the authority of masters alone. It matters because these are beliefs about what can injure and kill.
- ch. 21 "The Moving Shadow of Truth" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Aristotle, Michel Foucault, René Descartes — The Dialectic; Mind–Body Dualism; Embodiment (the lived body); Discipline and Docile Bodies — Haffner and Vogel define martial arts by a Wittgensteinian family resemblance to combat and organize the promise of self-improvement as paired opposites, working them Hegelian dialectic style, granting some truth to each side. They ask whether training brings peace or violence (Hobbes's shield for a war of all against all and Freudian catharsis versus Aristotle's worry that habituated violence breeds violence), strength fantasies or Socratic humility about weakness (with Sun Tzu's know-your-enemy and Foucault on the teacher's gaze and dojo power games), Cartesian dualism versus embodiment, and appreciation of tradition versus its distortion. The lesson is that the martial path holds both light and shadow, and separating enlightenment from self-deception takes eternal vigilance.
- ch. 22 "What Monkey Should Have Known" **·** The Buddha — Buddhism; Zen Buddhism; Karma and Rebirth — Mortensen opens with Monkey from Journey to the West beating six robbers to death despite Tripitaka's protest, and asks whether a practitioner of budo can be a Buddhist. He defends three principles, Take No Life, No First Strike and Stop Before Harm, qualifying them via the Upaya-kausalya Sutra's sea captain, Funakoshi's 'there is no first strike in karate', Ueshiba's purely defensive aikido, the initiator's bad karma, and the exception of multiple attackers; then he applies them to weapons, arguing that wooden weapons (the jo, Musashi's bokken, above all the humble walking stick, the 'last legal weapon') fit the precepts where the katana does not. Monkey, in short, should have carried a stick.
- ch. 23 "Living Beauty" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Pythagoras — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Yin and Yang — Saltzman explains why a flowing Shaolin Kenpo form is beautiful by way of Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: the Apollonian geometry of square, triangle and circle fuses with Dionysian power and intention, just as yang hardness needs yin softness. She grounds the body's fitness for this in the Golden Ratio known to Pythagoras, answers 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder' with Clive Bell's 'significant form' as an objective structure that trained judges can recognize, and locates 'living beauty' in the practitioner's own breakthrough, the moment when, as Nietzsche and Yeats agree, the dancer and the dance dissolve into pure mindless movement.
- ch. 24 "Excalibur - Western Martial Arts" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Jousting for Virtue" **·** Aristotle — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Farrell argues that the medieval code of chivalry is a living case study for Aristotle's virtue ethics: Lancelot, 'mekest in hall and sternest to his foe', embodies the paradox C.S. Lewis names as meek and fierce 'to the nth', which Farrell reads as Aristotle's courage, the golden mean between cowardice and rashness, exercised 'to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive'. The joust, meanwhile, was a proving ground where knightly virtues became second nature through habituated practice, since as Aristotle says 'it is no easy task to be good'. Western martial arts, he concludes, are 'moral kung fu': a fencing match with one's own standards of virtue.
- ch. 26 "Boxing, a School for Virtues" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean — Marino answers colleagues who call college boxing 'teaching violence' with an Aristotelian defense: courage is the mean between fearlessness and excessive fear, and the ring is one of the few workshops where fear is actually practiced. He cites Wacquant's boxing gym as 'a school of morality' in Durkheim's sense, Rotella's 'education at the fights', and boxers like Maja Cavlovic and George Foreman on how training takes over when fear hits, to argue boxing forges emotional self-command. His challenge to his own students: 'How can you be consistently honest or just if you don't have the mettle to take a hit?'
- ch. 27 "Is Fencing a Dishonorable Art" **·** Thomas Hobbes — Ethical Egoism; The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Michaud argues that fencing is the loneliest and most egoistic martial art: alone on the strip, you seek to understand your opponent only in order to deceive them through disengages and parry-feints. He maps the bout onto Hobbes: psychological egoism, the dueling ground as a state of nature of 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short', and the referee as the Leviathan whose rules keep the bloodshed out while licensing normative egoism inside them. Testing defenses from Rand, Friedman and Carr's business 'rules of the game', he concludes that fencing kept its soldier's anything-goes ethos after the lethal stakes vanished, making it a 'dishonorable' art: a Hobbesian feast of solitude, egoism and deception.
- ch. 28 "The Personality of the Épée" *(no index entry yet)* — Lawrence asks why anyone practices the épée, an 'unmartial martial art' with no self-defense payoff, one-sided exercise value, and only stylized descent from dueling to first blood (unlike foil and saber's artificial targets and right-of-attack rules). His three answers: fencing uniquely rewards psychology, timing and dexterity over strength and pain-endurance (he prefers Odysseus's guile to Ajax's force); it continues a Bronze-Age tradition ('the history of the sword is the history of mankind'); and the named swords of epic, from Excalibur to Sting, point to the weapon's distinctive personality of courage, honor, deadliness, aesthetic fitness for purpose, and an intimacy with the opponent that Housman's saber-duel poem captures.
- ch. 29 "Back to Square One" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jeremy Bentham — Moss concedes fencing's romantic dueling aura, noting that Kant classed a killing in a duel as mere manslaughter, Bentham proposed giving duelists the protection of self-defense for the sake of honor, and Rousseau and Schopenhauer sneered at the whole business. But he argues the sport's uniqueness lies not in honor, psychology or combat origins, which it shares with other martial arts, but in a combination of rules: the blade-set distance between fencers, protective gear that makes them effectively invulnerable, right-of-way, and the return to a neutral start after each point. That combination allows the complex 'phrases' of feint and disengage that make fencing 'physical chess'; what is unique, he concludes, is a matter of rules, not romance.
- ch. 30 "And in the Blue Corner, Wearing the White Pants" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "The University of Hard Knocks" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "Fighting Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 33 "Copyright Page" *(front)*

## Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

- ch. 1 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Faith and Reason — Editor Jorge Gracia's preface frames The Passion as a phenomenon that stirs people too deeply for indifference (a minister's fatal heart attack in a Brazilian cinema, reviews ranging from zero to five stars) and argues its religious stakes give its questions more bite than those of The Matrix or The Lord of the Rings. It lays out the book's five controversies: whether Christ had to suffer violently and what atonement means, whether the film is anti-Semitic, how faith relates to truth and to reading the Gospels as God's word, why Christ was killed, and whether Judas can be morally responsible for a betrayal God foreknew and redemption required. Gracia insists the collection takes no side and offers only a point of departure.
- ch. 8 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Thomas Aquinas — The Leap of Faith; Faith and Reason — McInerny argues Gibson's film works like Kierkegaard's indirect communication: its shocking graphic realism, against the tamed stations of the cross and serene crucifixes of Catholic churches, targets nominal Christians and forces each viewer to hear Jesus's 'I want you' and confront the scandal of the Incarnation rather than domesticate it. He reads the film alongside Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions as embroidery with no meaning apart from the Gospels, and invokes Aquinas on the Eucharist as the continuing memorial of the passion in which Christ is hidden under bread and wine. The film is 'a sign of contradiction' that, like Nietzsche's self-declared Antichrist, divides humanity into acceptance or rejection, so that efforts to keep religion within the bounds of reason alone must distort it.
- ch. 10 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Martin Heidegger, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Blaise Pascal, Albert Camus — Phenomenology; Embodiment (the lived body); The Absurd — Wrathall defends the film's violence by contrasting Fra Angelico's serene Descent from the Cross with Corinth's Red Christ and Gibson's Gethsemane rebuke ('You could not watch even one hour with me'), arguing the gore resists rationalizing Christ's suffering into an economy of exchange, as Camus's Father Paneloux in The Plague insists true faith must not. Drawing on Pascal's instrumental reason, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty, he develops a 'world-disclosive' account of faith: the tall-table scene between Mary and the young carpenter Jesus shows that new practices train new perception, and film reaches the body directly in ways written description cannot. He closes by faulting Gibson for pessimism: Christ's world looks as God-forsaken and demon-haunted as Judas's, closer to Dostoevsky's ascetic Father Ferapont than to a world made new.
- ch. 12 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Anselm of Canterbury, Immanuel Kant, Augustine of Hippo — Forgiveness; Faith and Reason — Walls argues the controversy lies not in the gore but in who died on the cross and why, and shows Gibson weaving the three classic atonement theories: Christ crushing the serpent in Gethsemane as the Christus-Victor ransom (with Augustine's mousetrap image), the Isaiah 53 scourging and Gibson's own hand driving the nail as Anselm-style penal substitution in which the innocent dies so the guilty Barabbas in each of us goes free, and the transformed characters (Mary Magdalene, Simon of Cyrene, the good thief, the kneeling soldier) as Abelard's moral influence. Against Kant's charge that atonement is a superstitious substitute for moral transformation, he cites Swinburne and Quinn: pleading the atonement requires repentance, and the tens of thousands of reported conversions and confessions show it transforms lives. He concludes that any adequate account needs all three theories, objective payment and subjective transformation alike, and that atonement aims at mercy and reconciliation rather than retribution.
- ch. 13 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Humanity as an End in Itself; Forgiveness — Taliaferro, writing as a personalist, worries that Gibson's relentless focus on torture eclipses the whole person of Christ: like torture victims losing peripheral vision, viewers lose sight of his teaching, healings, nonviolence, and resurrection, and the satisfaction-theology framing risks relishing redemptive suffering itself. His reconciliation thought-experiment (Patricia's betrayal of Kris and the God-man who resurrects the murdered child) argues that the resurrection, not the passion alone, completes at-one-ment, since no amount of suffering can undo past wrong. He contrasts Gandalf's laughing return in The Return of the King with a Gibson Jesus who could not plausibly laugh after rising, and invokes Scheler's St. Francis, who loves the wholeness behind sickness rather than the sickness, to urge that the film's intensity edges out a life-affirming view of persons as irreducibly valuable in themselves.
- ch. 14 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle, Plato — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Irwin defends the film's violence aesthetically: beauty (Michelangelo's Pietà) distracts from moral truth rather than serving it, and Aristotle's Poetics fits the film neither as tragedy (a flawless Christ cannot fall through hamartia, and a good man's fall from prosperity is 'repulsive', so no catharsis explains why we watch) nor as the Plato-banned spectacle that inflames the passions, since it leaves viewers numb rather than belligerent. Instead he applies Cynthia Freeland's four features of the cinematic sublime, drawn from Burke and Kant: the flogging scenes, the grotesque Satan clutching his deformed child, Judas harried by demon-children to suicide, and even the Aramaic and Latin subtitles produce the pain-pleasure conflict, overwhelming vastness, and jolt from feeling to moral reflection that make the experience sublime. The violence is thus justified as Gibson's deliberate delivery of the sublime, provided viewers leave fear at the gates.
- ch. 15 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Blaise Pascal, Thomas Hobbes, Friedrich Nietzsche — Master–Slave Dialectic; The Dialectic; Geist (World Spirit) — Lawler charges that Gibson's atonement theology, in which the more barbaric the torture the greater the redemption, imprisons Christianity at the stage of Hegel's 'Unhappy Consciousness', where an infinite God is sundered from abject sinful humanity and a priestly mediator is needed. Reading the film through the master-slave dialectic (impotent master Pilate versus the dignified slave Simon of Cyrene; the world of separate egos as Hobbes's war of all against all), he argues that what dies on the cross is the separate ego itself, and that what rises is Geist, the 'I' that is 'We' of the loving human community. Against Tertullian's credo quia absurdum, and using Pascal's 'heart has its reasons' alongside Hegel's dialectical reason, he reads 'you are gods' and the prodigal son as teaching every person's essential divinity, so the film's own art (the Mater Dolorosa, our identification with the flesh-and-blood Jesus) implicitly undermines the separatist theology Gibson intends.
- ch. 16 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Wartenberg recounts a Mount Holyoke panel where a New Testament historian, a scholar of Jewish mysticism, campus ministers, and a film theorist effectively saw different movies, and proposes that the film itself divides into 'The Passion of the Condemnation' (where a humane, tormented Pilate caves to bloodthirsty Jewish crowds, complete with the Matthew 27:25 blood-guilt line left untranslated for American test audiences) and 'The Passion of the Crucifixion' (the two-hour torture that true believers experience as their God's willing sacrifice, overwhelming everything before it). He then explains the split audience through cinema's photographic verisimilitude: just as D.W. Griffith's The Birth of a Nation used documentary-style realism to pass Klan apologetics off as history, Gibson's brutally realistic violence lends his slanted, Emmerich-inflected narrative the authority of fact. He rejects the postmodernist consolation that all readings are equally valid, insisting believers were manipulated by the medium's false trustworthiness.
- ch. 18 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Philosophical Skepticism; Faith and Reason; Democracy — Kurtz, the secular humanist, argues the film is a political weapon of the Religious Right (O'Reilly, Dobson, Gingrich) that presents fantasy as fact: Gibson claims fidelity to the Gospels while borrowing torture scenes such as the bridge plunge and the savage flogging from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, whitewashing the historical Pilate, and erasing that Jesus, Mary, and the disciples were themselves Jews. Applying historical criticism, he contends the Gospels are anonymous, second- and third-hand missionary propaganda written forty to seventy years after Jesus, shaped by the rivalry between rabbinic Judaism and Gentile-seeking Jewish Christianity and canonized politically at Nicaea under Constantine. He concludes by defending the freedom of inquiry, skeptical scrutiny of all sacred texts, and the First Amendment's separation of church and state against the film's power to inflame anti-Semitism and the American culture war.
- ch. 19 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Corlett applies the ethics of racism, due process, responsibility, and punishment to the film: he argues The Passion is not racist because it depicts dissenting Sanhedrin members, the supportive Simon of Cyrene, and the Jewish Mary and Jesus, so blame falls on individual wrongdoers like Caiaphas rather than on Jews as a group, and audiences' misreadings are not the artist's fault. He catalogs the violations of due process (guilty-until-proven-innocent before the Sanhedrin, beatings en route to the hearing, the swap for the convicted killer Barabbas) and the failure to separate religious from civil authority. On punishment he defends a principle of proportionality and desert: Jesus's innocence made his torture and execution unjust, but abuse does not negate proper use, so the film gives no argument against capital punishment per se while giving evildoers who escape earthly justice their deserts only if God is just.
- ch. 20 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** William James, Plato — Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Faith and Reason — Bronson argues Gibson's fixation on Jesus's suffering is not a Christian oddity but a deeply Jewish mystical one: using William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity), he reads the Gethsemane opening, where Jesus crushes Satan's serpent and receives a vision of the Father, as a classic mystical trial in the line of Moses at Sinai, Daniel's chariot-throne vision, Elijah's fiery ascent, John the Baptist, Paul's blinding light, and later the Kabbalah and Hasidic masters whose path to God runs through anguish. The Platonic Socrates of the Symposium and Phaedrus (wisdom arriving through the madness of love) and the medieval agreement of al-Ghazali, Maimonides, and Aquinas that reason cannot reach God frame his philosophy-versus-mysticism contrast, including the film's mother-son floorboard scene as love but not full mystical contact. The added scene where Pilate's wife tells him 'If you will not hear the truth, no one can tell you' shows Gibson siding with the mystical path to truth over Pilate's pragmatic one.
- ch. 21 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Martin Heidegger, Friedrich Nietzsche, William James, Jean Baudrillard — Perspectivism; Truth as What Works; The Leap of Faith — Irwin takes Pilate's Quid est veritas as a guided tour of theories of truth applied to the film: Gibson's sympathetic Pilate embodies relativism, met with Nietzsche's 'truth is a woman' perspectivism and Baudrillard's postmodern laughter and rejected; Caiaphas and the bad thief demanding Jesus come down from the cross put the correspondence theory to work ('the proof is out there'), though beliefs hang on other beliefs ad infinitum; Simon of Cyrene's growing conviction models the coherence theory, exposed as necessary but not sufficient by Swinburne's case for versus Wells's case against the divinity of Jesus; and Pilate's Barabbas gambit parodies James's pragmatic theory, where working is not enough if there is no corresponding reality. He then retrieves Heidegger's reading of aletheia as uncovering, helped by the Quid est veritas anagram ('Est qui vir adest': it is the man before you) and Gadamer on truth seizing us like beauty, so that Jesus's 'I am the truth' and Claudia's dream-guided warnings point to truth as disclosure. Since disclosure alone cannot decide between inconsistent revealed claims, Irwin ends by leaving the viewer with a leap of faith and a first instinct as final answer.
- ch. 23 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Thomas Aquinas — Faith and Reason — Jorge Gracia reframes the fidelity controversy as a problem in the theory of interpretation: Gibson had to make countless choices the Gospels leave silent (Christ's worn clothing, the Italian landscape, Jesus staring into the camera at the Last Supper, added scenes like Satan raging and demon children haunting Judas), so the film is unavoidably an interpretation. He surveys five criteria interpreters of Scripture have used — personal intuition (illustrated by Augustine's 'take and read' in the Confessions), ecclesial authority and the visions of nuns Emmerich and Agreda, sola scriptura, historical scholarship, and tradition (Aquinas's camp; Veronica's veil, the Shroud, the virgin Mary's prominence) — and argues each is inadequate alone because every one rests on prior theology. Hence disputes about the film are really disputes between theologies, and the film makes sense only within Gibson's Catholic view of Jesus as the Messiah announced by Isaiah 53.
- ch. 24 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings, Immanuel Kant — The Ethics of Care; Feminism; Objectification; Caring as the Ground of Ethics — Cynthia Freeland reads the film's women through feminist ethics of care: the two Marys function like a Greek-chorus of grieving observers, while Claudia and Veronica — and the casting of Bellucci as the repentant whore opposite Morgenstern's ageless Madonna — lock them into the virgin/whore double bind. Using Carol Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg's Kantian standard and Nel Noddings's and Sara Ruddick's point that mothering is reflective 'attentive' work, she argues Gibson's Mary is one-dimensional: flashbacks of 'I am here' show maternal instinct, never moral deliberation. She ends by suggesting the historical Jesus, like Socrates, was more radical toward women than the film, and that Irigaray's reading of Christ's bleeding wounds as a feminized maternal body sits oddly with Gibson's muscular, 'take it like a man' Savior.
- ch. 25 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Plato, Aristotle — Faith and Reason; The Problem of Evil; Existence Precedes Essence — Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.
- ch. 27 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Socrates, Plato — Immortality and the Soul; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Gareth Matthews contrasts Plato's serene Phaedo — Socrates conducting a seminar on immortality, death as the cure for life's ills, 'we owe a cock to Asclepius' — with Gibson's prolonged torture, while noting deep parallels: both men were condemned by large courts on religious charges (impiety, blasphemy) with political subtexts. Socrates in the Apology models facing death through Socratic ignorance ('to fear death is to think oneself wise when one is not'), and Matthews argues Gibson's magnified suffering makes Christ an icon of an atonement nobody could imitate rather than a model for our own deaths; only the Gethsemane prayer and 'why hast thou forsaken me' (read via Cullmann) can actually help a believer face dying.
- ch. 28 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Martin Heidegger, Anselm of Canterbury, Socrates — Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity; The Meaning of Life — Bruce Reichenbach reads the film's choreographed pas de deux as three distinct theories of atonement: the conquest dance with Satan in Gethsemane (crushing the serpent of Genesis 3:15, Satan's final scream) enacts the Christus victor view of the Church Fathers; Simon of Cyrene's reluctant co-bearing of the cross illustrates Abelard's moral-influence view, though Gibson shows resilient fortitude rather than the love Abelard's theory requires to transform Simon; and Mary's mirrored 'parallel dance' makes her a co-redemptrix sharing her son's agony. Against this he sets Heidegger — Jesus grasps his death with anticipatory resolve, thrownness, and the 'moment of vision' with Mary, but dies for the Other rather than to authenticate his own life — and faults the film for omitting Anselm's (and Swinburne's) substitutionary atonement entirely: no sin, repentance, reparation, or penance appears, unlike Maximilian Kolbe's real substitution at Auschwitz.
- ch. 29 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Faith and Reason; The Problem of Evil — Paul Moser answers the objection that an all-loving God could not plan His Son's torture by arguing the cross is God's scandalous self-giving love: Jesus is no mere moral guru but the unique atoning sacrifice (the mad/Satanic/Son-of-God trilemma, 'he who delivered me to you has the greater sin'), and the crucifixion is God's grand reversal where self-giving love defeats death. He attacks the 'nice god' of natural theology as domesticating idolatry — God hides His plans from 'the wise and the intelligent' — and holds that we know God not by philosophical evidence but through Gethsemane-style filial obedience ('not my will but yours'), noting that Gibson himself appears in the film driving a nail, casting all of us as the crucifiers whom God forgives.
- ch. 30 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Friedrich Nietzsche, Arthur Schopenhauer — Free Will vs Determinism; Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Jonathan Sanford distinguishes necessity of the end, of compulsion, and of nature to argue Christ's passion was both necessary and free: justice requires reparation for the harmony Adam and Eve broke, God cannot simply waive it without making a mockery of sin, yet no compulsion operates on Christ — unlike the blind inner drives Nietzsche's will to power or Schopenhauer's will would represent. Using Aristotle, he argues Christ's fully virtuous character (practical wisdom plus courage and temperance become a 'second nature') makes disobedience nearly unimaginable, and his divinity makes it impossible, so his choice 'could not have been different' precisely because it was perfectly free; the Gethsemane agony shows not division in the God-man but the difficulty of holding his human and divine wills in unity.
- ch. 32 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Boethius, Harry Frankfurt, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — Fate and Foreknowledge; Compatibilism; Virtue Ethics; Utilitarianism — Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.
- ch. 33 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant — Faith and Reason; Utilitarianism; Deontology — Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.
- ch. 34 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 35 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 36 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Mr. Monk and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Mr. Monk Meets Alexander the Great" **·** Albert Camus, Diogenes the Cynic — The Myth of Sisyphus; The Absurd; Cynicism (living according to nature); Rebellion and Revolt — Wittkower argues that Monk's daily, unwinnable war on dirt and disorder is Camus's happy Sisyphus made concrete: Monk vacuums ceilings, touches lampposts, and solves murders knowing the dirt and the murderers will always return ('There's never hope... Hope. I hate hope's guts' in 'Mr. Monk Can't See a Thing'), yet he still finds enough satisfaction to take up the wipe again. Reading Ecclesiastes' vanity alongside the uncaring wasp of the opening, the chapter claims Monk shows us how to live wisely without resignation in an absurd world that does not care. He is paired with Diogenes the Cynic, whose barrel, raw onions, and midday lantern mirror Monk's pot-pie-Tuesdays and his refusal to overlook what everyone else ignores; like Diogenes telling Alexander the Great 'get out of my sun,' Monk lives by his own ideals no matter how society judges him. The essay closes that, like Camus addressing the Dominican monks, we should refuse to 'be reasonable' about evil and disorder and keep struggling without hope, wipe in hand.
- ch. 7 "I Just Solved the Case - How Monk Think" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "It’s a Gift ... and a Curse" **·** Edmund Husserl, Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Phenomenology — Welsh argues Monk's 'gift and curse' is being permanently stuck in Husserl's phenomenological attitude. Selective-attention experiments (the swapped interviewer behind the door, the gorilla-suit walker) show that the rest of us see only what expectation renders possible, while Monk, like Poe's Dupin finding the Purloined Letter in plain sight, brackets his assumptions and actually perceives: the moved decorative rock in Dr. Kroger's courtyard, the wing-back chair and wiped bullets proving the 'suicide' in 'Mr. Monk and the Garbage Strike' is murder, and the illiterate suspect's English-sign slip in 'Mr. Monk Goes to a Fashion Show' — all through his hand-framing 'Zen Sherlock Holmes thing.' But because he cannot exit back into the natural attitude, the same perception is pathological. Drawing on Damasio's Descartes' Error and Merleau-Ponty's patient Schneider, the chapter argues that emotion is what structures relevance and action, so Monk's refusal to let emotional bonds organize his life leaves him isolated and unhappy — though curing the curse might cost him the gift that solves the cases.
- ch. 9 "Is Monk’s Certainty Justified" **·** Karl Popper, René Descartes — Falsificationism; The Best of All Possible Worlds; Ockham's Razor — Rauhut tests Monk's method against two models of discovery: Holmes-style eliminatism, modeled on Popper's falsification via reductio ad absurdum, and CSI-style confirmationism in the mold of Hempel and Carnap (Gil Grissom letting evidence speak). Monk fits neither — in 'Mr. Monk and the Astronaut' he refuses to eliminate the alibi-solid Steve Wagner, and in 'Mr. Monk Falls in Love' he ignores a hatpin, a motive, and a confession pointing at Leyla. Instead Monk is an 'epiphanist': he registers every anomaly (the secretary hired from a Lamaze-class ad in 'Mr. Monk Fights City Hall', Crawford's odd phrasing 'No, she wouldn't be drinking now'), suddenly sees the one theory explaining all of them, and only afterwards manufactures shareable evidence for others. His absolute certainty, the chapter argues, rests on a metaphysical faith that only the true theory can explain every anomaly — a Leibnizian 'best of all possible ordered worlds' — the same obsession with order that makes him notice anomalies at all, though it makes him epistemically irresponsible by ordinary standards that weigh alternative hypotheses and simplicity.
- ch. 10 "Step Back" **·** David Hume — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; Problem of Induction — Gallagher uses Monk's phobias to test Hume's claim that believing is itself a kind of feeling. The chapter asks whether a fear conflicting with a rational belief (Monk paralyzed by the possibly-on stove during a murder investigation) feels any different from a conflict between two fears ('Snakes trump heights' in 'Mr. Monk and the Very, Very Old Man') or two beliefs, and answers with Hume that beliefs are forceful-feeling representations — there is a 'what it's like' to believing the German shepherd is dangerous. On Hume's account the force of a belief comes from repetition of experience, which explains both why Monk's fears should fade (countless safely landed flights, millions of milk drinkers) and why they persist: his mind dwells repeatedly on the rare catastrophe, giving fearful representations extra force, as when his repeated experience that 'she's always cheating' makes him wrongly believe Brody's wife in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully.' The practical lesson is to step back and widen attention to all the possibilities, as Monk intermittently manages with the help of Natalie and Stottlemeyer.
- ch. 11 "He’s the Guy - What Monk Is Made Of" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "You Don’t Have to Be Like Him to Like Him" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); The Golden Mean; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Levitt reads Monk through Aristotle's virtue ethics: a man of character whose police virtues survive Trudy's murder but whose phobias produce akrasia — in the pilot he knows he must descend the germ-filled sewer to save Sharona and freezes anyway, doing the right thing only at agonizing cost. Virtue as habit and the golden mean (friendliness as the mean between obsequiousness and standoffishness) frame his slow progress toward acting rightly without thinking, which is also why Stottlemeyer cannot recommend his reinstatement — he doubts the illness, not the man. Aristotle's three friendships sort Monk's relationships: utility (the department, employer Sharona), pleasure, and virtue — Natalie, who after watching Monk save Julie's fish over the priceless moon rock saw her late husband's goodness in him. Ethos, pathos, logos and catharsis then explain viewer identification: watching Monk move from akrasia toward balance (Dr. Kroger's 'N. Hope' note that turns out to mean New Hope) lets audiences identify with, and be ennobled by, a character we would never want to be.
- ch. 13 "It’s Time for the Other Walkie-Talkie" **·** Aristotle, Plato, Seneca, Michel de Montaigne — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Philosophy of Love; Stoicism — Dodge puts Monk on the case of friendship's nature, structured by Aristotle's three kinds from the Nicomachean Ethics: Hal Tucker's fake buddy act in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend' is pure utility, while Natalie's is virtue-friendship — she is his friend 'in spite of' the job since 'he doesn't pay her that much.' The friend as mirror and 'second self' grounds the claim that Stottlemeyer, Sharona, Natalie and Randy reflect Monk's excellence back to him, and Bacon's point that a friend redoubles joys and cuts griefs in half is shown when they stay up all night during his suicide watch. Seneca's Stoic counsel — judge a person long before admitting him, then hold nothing back — is exemplified by Natalie's fish-over-moon-rock test of Monk's character, while Montaigne's once-in-centuries friendship in which two selves blur fits only Trudy, whose dying words 'bread and butter' tell Monk they belong together. Plato's Lysis (the 'great cosmic swirly' Monk cites in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully') opens the puzzle Socrates could not solve, and the single walkie-talkie his father gave him shows why the chapter's verdict — Monk now has friends — matters.
- ch. 14 "Mr. Monk’s Greatness" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre, Plato — The Übermensch; Existence Precedes Essence — Lewis argues Monk is Nietzsche's Übermensch. Sketching Sartre's existence-precedes-essence through the contrast between the designed wipe and self-defining humans, the chapter claims Monk creates his own essence through choices — keeping the coffee table askew in memory of Trudy, 'dirtying' his house in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend,' drinking stream water in 'Mr. Monk Gets Cabin Fever' — and lives by self-prescribed values (hourly flossing, bagged tissues, relentless truth-seeking) that separate him from the herd of the Court of Public Opinion. The comparison with Stottlemeyer — Nietzsche's lookalike with the mustache, 'the quintessential man' of the herd — inverts the expected hierarchy: 'He was a yardstick for me, of both detection and character' ('Mr. Monk Goes to Mexico') shows the badge-carrying everyman is the inferior one. Monk therefore challenges the macho sci-fi stereotype of the superman: the Übermensch can be gentle and kind, fight for truth and a cleaner world, and still have room to improve ('What does not kill me makes me stronger').
- ch. 15 "Unless I’m Wrong, and I’m Not... - Monk’s Logic" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Mr. Monk Is Mr. Monk" **·** John Locke, David Hume, Thomas Reid — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Bundle Theory of Self — Malloy runs the classic theories of personal identity through Monk episodes. Bodily (really brain) identity fails when 'the Monk' — the reckless medicated alter of 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' — shares Monk's body and brain yet is not held responsible, and Stanley Tucci's method actor in 'Mr. Monk and the Actor' shows that copying Monk's looks and behavior does not transfer identity. Locke's memory theory breaks on the amnesia of 'Mr. Monk Bumps His Head' (Monk becomes roofer 'Jerry') and the blackout in 'Mr. Monk and the Rapper,' and Reid's brave-officer paradox yields contradiction once recovered Monk remembers being both Monk and Jerry. Hume's bundle theory — 'I never can catch myself,' the self as theatre of successive perceptions — grounds psychological continuity's graded identity, but then cult-swayed Monk in 'Mr. Monk Joins a Cult' might count as a different person, making his deprogramming a kind of murder; the chapter closes by rejecting Reid and Butler's 'simple and unassayable' escape, insisting a philosopher, like a detective, must keep theorizing how Monk stays Monk.
- ch. 17 "Here’s How It Happened and Didn’t Happen" *(no index entry yet)* — Michaud asks how TV's most logical detective can assert contradictions: Monk says 'I know it's impossible, but he's the guy' about Derek Philby murdering while proctoring an exam ('Mr. Monk Goes Back to School') and about astronaut Steve Wagner killing while in orbit ('Mr. Monk and the Astronaut'), seeming violations of the Law of Non-Contradiction that his own valid arguments (the missing glass of water ruling out suicide) depend on. The chapter stages Graham Priest's dialetheism — the Liar Sentence as a true contradiction — as a possible defense, even borrowing Gricean maxims to argue Monk would announce a dialetheia if he believed one, but concludes Monk never actually accepts true contradictions: the impossible accusation creates a tension that drives him to find the hidden mechanism (Wagner's pre-rigged garage door), so the 'contradiction' dissolves once a false assumption is exposed. Michaud's closing suggestion is that the Liar Sentence itself should be treated as a crime to be solved rather than a dialetheia to be accepted.
- ch. 18 "Here’s What Happened" **·** The Myth of Sisyphus — Kane, a catalog librarian, argues that Monk's detecting mirrors library cataloging. Monk 'collocates' — identical boxes on one wall, a row of matching Trudy photos on another — and reasons user-first, exactly as Cutter's rule says to choose the entry a library's users will look under first: in 'Mr. Monk and the Bad Girlfriend' he sees the suspect with no alibi must be innocent because a killer who hides in the bathroom already has an alibi secured. Like the invisible cataloger, Monk imposes the order others see without knowing someone arranged it, and both face Sisyphus's rock: Monk's control ends at his apartment door ('Mr. Monk Makes the Playoffs' tailgate chaos), and Universal Bibliographic Control — one standard for describing every work ever created — will never stay at the top of the hill. The Cutter-versus-Dewey rivalry parallels Monk versus Harold Krenshaw, the flashy thunder-stealer who gets famous first, and the chapter ends by pronouncing Monk a natural-born cataloger.
- ch. 19 "He’s a Iteal Character - Monk Competition" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Identity" *(no index entry yet)* — Zaffran reads Monk and Dr. House as twin heirs of Sherlock Holmes — impossible crimes versus impossible diseases — both 'marked' like Oedipus, the first fictional detective, whose truth-seeking destroyed him: Monk's OCD begins with the unsolved murder of Trudy, which he feels implicated in, while House's limp, addiction and misanthropy trace to a misdiagnosis and childhood abuse. The chapter's core argument uses Bachelard's Prometheus complex, 'the Oedipus complex of intellectual life': both sleuths are punished for their insight, chained like Prometheus to their disorders (OCD; Vicodin and the bad leg), yet keep stealing the fire of explanation — their real goal is not justice or cure but disclosing the hidden how of each murder and disease. Monk and House are ultimately mirrors of their writers and audience: fiction (via Brian Boyd's evolutionary account) lets us rehearse moral situations and appease our fear of boredom, which is why we love these gift-and-curse characters and keep coming back for the next episode.
- ch. 21 "The Emotion-Reason Dilemma, Part II" **·** Michel Foucault — Feminism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Pribram places Monk and Dr. House in the tradition of the brilliantly rational but emotionally plagued detective (Dragnet's emotionless Joe Friday vs Cracker's Fitz), arguing both shows treat excessive emotion as the price of genius: Monk's OCD is tied to his pattern-spotting ('You're a freak of nature'), and when medication cures the OCD in 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' his detective genius vanishes. She applies Foucault's Birth of the Clinic to House's subtracting of the patient, but shows both series critique that modernist rationality through Eve in 'One Day, One Room', who forces House to face the rationally inexplicable. Using feminist scholarship (Jaggar, Alberti, Battersby), she argues the opposition of male reason to female emotion is a historically specific construction, and offers the best friends Stottlemeyer and Wilson as integrated alternatives who pay for their balance with ordinariness: polarization equals greatness, integration signals the mundane.
- ch. 22 "Herr Leibniz Consoles Mr. Monk" **·** Gottfried Leibniz, Ludwig Wittgenstein — The Best of All Possible Worlds; Principle of Sufficient Reason; Monadology — Kavas distinguishes Monk's method from Holmes's modus ponens, Poirot's elimination, and Goren's profiling: Monk accepts only what completes a coherent total narrative, so 'Here's what happened' re-tells the order of the whole world, as in the chess-game solution of 'Mr. Monk and the Genius'. The chapter uses the Tractatus's world of contingent, logically independent facts to model Monk's picture-completion, then brings in Leibniz: the principle of sufficient reason, the best of all possible worlds, and preestablished harmony justify Monk's faith that even Trudy's death must have a reason. Monk emerges as a pessimistic Leibniz who takes the world to be the worst possible precisely because, since learning the bomb was meant for Trudy in 'Mr. Monk Goes to Jail', he cannot see any sufficient reason for her death ('Why her?').
- ch. 23 "He’s ... Not Like Everyone Else - The Spiritual Side of Adrian Monk" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Does the Habit Make the Monk" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Anselm of Canterbury, Aristotle — The Ontological Argument; The Five Ways — Elliott maps the recurring Monk stalemate onto medieval theology: in 'Mr. Monk Goes to the Circus', Stottlemeyer and Disher reason forward from a hunch and the evidence, exactly like Anselm's ontological argument, which assumes what it sets out to prove, while Monk, like Aquinas against Anselm, refuses assumptions and reasons backward from verifiable facts, asking why an assassin would somersault except to advertise the acrobatic alibi. Aquinas's First Cause argument (Aristotle's unmoved mover) supplies the model of proving a certainty from observable things, paralleling Monk's 'I don't know how he did it, but he did it' backward deduction. The chapter's closing move likens Monk to the medieval monks themselves: his OCD-driven ascetic withdrawal from the dirty, chaotic world (contemptus mundi) is what lets him notice the imperfection in scenes like the locker room of 'Mr. Monk and the Big Game' that reveals sabotage.
- ch. 25 "Shaman, Heal Thyself" *(no index entry yet)* — Culver reads Monk as a shamanic figure in Arnold van Gennep's and Victor Turner's sense: a liminal man, neither cop nor civilian, fixed in the transitional stage of mourning Trudy, who heals society's disorder from its margins as Holmes and Poirot did. Drawing on Mary Douglas's Purity and Danger (dirt as defilement and disorder), she interprets Monk's ritualized gestures and utterances, framing the scene with his hands, the rare solving-smile, 'he's the guy' and 'Here's what happened', as the ceremonial performance by which disorder is overcome. Episodes like 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' and 'Mr. Monk Joins a Cult' then show the shaman's bind: whenever Monk attains purity or happiness he loses his sacred gift, so he must refuse to heal himself and remain 'a blessing and a curse'.
- ch. 26 "Mr. Monk Murdered Trudy" **·** The Buddha — Compassion (karuna); Emptiness (sunyata); Non-Self (anatman) — Green argues Monk is an unintentional Bodhisattva whose OCD enacts the Four Bodhisattva Vows: the compulsion to touch lampposts is the first vow's blind desires, his monastic minimalism the Dharma gate, and his crime-solving compassion for a disordered world the third vow, with the Dhammapada's teaching that the untamed mind produces suffering exemplified by Monk and by Harold Krenshaw's rival ordering. Like Vimalakirti feigning illness, or Shawn Spencer in Psych, and like the father in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable, Monk and his writers use skillful deception to awaken viewers to suffering and loving kindness. The title thesis is that Monk cannot solve Trudy's murder because he accepts responsibility for it: by Thich Nhat Hanh's Interbeing there is no absolute self and other, so solving the case requires the Zen 'kill the Buddha' eradication of the self, Monk's nirvana-as-extinction and the end of the series.
- ch. 27 "Our Hour Isn’t Over Yet, It’s Only Been Fifty-Eight Minutes - Monk in Therapy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "16 - Mr. Mead Starts Couples Therapy" *(no index entry yet)* — Clinical psychologist Sylvia Randall writes a thinly fictionalized case study in which 'Andrew Mead' (Monk: wife Terry killed violently, severe OCD, assistants Sheila/Sharona and Naomi/Natalie) brings his working relationships to couples therapy. Through 'I statements' and gentle confrontation, the sessions surface unconscious associations: Mead's fear that his father left because of him, his mother's OCD, Sheila's 'suck it up' childhood, and his survivor's guilt over joy since Terry's death, which an imagined conversation with Terry releases. The chapter's argument is the psychodynamic one that making unconscious material conscious lowers its emotional charge, widening the client's behavioral repertoire and restoring empathy and intimacy in the couple.
- ch. 29 "Mr. Monk, Jungle Guide" **·** Aristotle, The Buddha — Kagan reads Monk through Ernest Becker's Denial of Death: everyone is born hyper-aware like Monk and learns 'how not to see', managing the terror of the jungle out there through denial, shopping, and hero systems, which is why Randy Disher can ride in a cab driven by a corpse without noticing. Monk, who cannot forget (his nudity phobia traced to the trauma of his own birth in 'Mr. Monk and the Naked Man'), is our funhouse mirror and, like the Buddha seeing the four sights of sickness, old age, death, and the renunciant, he re-enters the world after Trudy's death to guide us through it. Aristotle's catharsis explains the pleasure of watching: pity and fear are burned off as Monk, more afraid than we are, still pursues truth and justice.
- ch. 30 "The Strength to Mourn" **·** Jacques Derrida — Tarantino and Wittkower read Monk through Freud's Beyond the Pleasure Principle: repetition compulsion (the fort/da child, the anxiety dream of running toward Trudy's car in 'Mr. Monk Is on the Run, Part 1') is the mind's attempt to retroactively prepare for trauma, which explains both the nudity phobia traced to Monk's birth and his endless return to Trudy's case. Monk's compulsions are also displacement behavior, standing in for the one disorder he cannot put in order, Trudy's death itself, which resists mourning because the beloved object cannot be de-cathected, a Derridean impossible mourning that leaves him haunted. Only when solving the crime proves empty does Monk reach the chapter's conclusion: happiness lies not in possessing lost objects of desire but in new emotional investment in a changing, uncertain world, which the authors name hope.

## Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

- ch. 1 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors introduce the volume by reading Gaiman's fiction as travel literature: heroes like Richard Mayhew in Neverwhere, Coraline, and Shadow in American Gods are forced or seduced into enchanted worlds that press against the mundane, and must map and decode those worlds to survive, transforming themselves in the process. They contrast tourists, who stay detached behind camera and guidebook, with travelers, who engage and are changed, and argue that reading Gaiman philosophically turns readers into travelers. They close with Gaiman's Newbery speech about stories as 'good lies that say true things' that leave readers changed forever.
- ch. 8 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, Seneca — Philosophical Skepticism; Free Will vs Determinism — Elizabeth Swanstrom reads Mr. Wednesday's recruitment of Shadow in American Gods as a two-man con that exploits Hume's account of causation: because the mind projects causal links from constant conjunction, Odin and Loki stage a chain of 'coincidences' (Laura's death, rerouted flights, the first-class seat) and use classic misdirection, from Sweeney's warning at Jack's Crocodile Bar to the Herodotus tale of Croesus, so that the mark never looks at the hand with the coin in it. Setting Hume's billiard-ball analysis against Seneca and the Stoic idea of derivative causality, she argues Wednesday manipulates association rather than chance itself. Shadow's counter-training in coin sleights, especially the Sucker Vanish, and Sweeney's gift of the resurrection coin that revives Laura introduce genuine chance, letting Shadow see the set-up, stop the sacrificial battle, and demonstrate that a causally saturated world still leaves room to break the game.
- ch. 10 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Tripartite Soul; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Greg Littmann stages Plato's hypothetical review of American Gods under the Republic's charges against poetry: the novel is full of 'greatest of all lies' about gods behaving badly, from Odin and Loki's sacrificial plot to Czernobog's head-smashing, gods degrading themselves into lesser forms like Horus the road-kill-eating hawk and Media as Lucille Ball, and characters ruled by passion rather than reason, from Mad Sweeney drinking himself to death to Thor's suicide, corrupting a soul that should be governed by rationality. Against this he sets Aristotle's Poetics: listening to music and intellectual leisure are valuable in themselves, fiction is more philosophic than history because it shows what could happen, the impossible is justified when it astounds, and catharsis through pity for figures like the weeping Mad Sweeney purges rather than corrupts. Because American Gods' absurd premise unfolds with internally probable, character-consistent events (loyal Shadow, loving Laura, grifter Odin), it satisfies Aristotle's requirement that fantasy make artistic sense.
- ch. 11 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** John Dewey — Pragmatism; Truth as What Works — Ray Bossert reads American Gods as an allegory of American philosophy: like Gaiman's gods, American philosophers labor invisibly in the background while European publics canonize their thinkers, and Shadow's prison exchanges show the point, since Loki must beg him to read Herodotus ('It's cool') while Johnnie Larch's 'don't piss off people who work in airports' beats Shadow's abstract generalization in usefulness. Following Hickman's Deweyan instrumentalism, he argues the gods are survival tools humans craft from need and discard when obsolete, so Czernobog's hammer gives way to Media's television, Wednesday treats even his own son as an instrument, and the buffalo man's 'believe everything' is advice about keeping one's tools of survival working. The chapter ends on liberty: Shadow refuses to be a god because 'we don't need anyone to believe in us,' and in the Egyptian death trial he claims the most American reward, the freedom to choose his own afterlife.
- ch. 12 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Gottfried Leibniz, David Chalmers, René Descartes — Theory of Forms; Monadology; The Hard Problem of Consciousness; Allegory of the Cave — Richard Rosenbaum asks how Gaiman's gods, abstract concepts made flesh who live or die by human belief, could exist, starting from Plato's Forms (Odin as personified battle-wisdom, Media as media) and the Allegory of the Cave, which gives new meaning to a protagonist literally named Shadow. Finding Forms too independent to need believers, he upgrades the metaphysics with Leibniz's Monadology: if everything, bodies and ideas alike, is composed of perception-bearing monads, then shared beliefs can agglomerate, 'level up' into a soul, and become a living god walking around America. Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness, panprotopsychism, and the claim that information has interdependent physical and phenomenal aspects supply the final mechanism, so collective belief realized phenomenally must become physically embodied, in contrast to the dualism of Descartes that made mind-body interaction mysterious.
- ch. 13 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, George Berkeley, Zhuangzi, Bertrand Russell, David Chalmers — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Zhuangzi's Perspectivism (butterfly dream); Philosophical Zombies — T. Bradley Richards takes The Sandman's Dreamworld seriously as a hypothesis: could our nightly dreams be travels to a mind-independent place like Morpheus's realm? Starting from Zhuangzi's butterfly dream and Descartes's dream argument, he uses Berkeley's God-sustained idealism as a model for how Morpheus's mind could uphold the Dreamworld's order, and a thought experiment about glitchy dream-travel defuses Descartes's appeal to the discontinuity of dreams. Against the objection that dreams are blatantly contradictory ('it was Dave, but it also wasn't Dave'), he deploys Russell's theory of descriptions against Meinongian subsistence, Chalmers-style conceivability-implies-possibility reasoning from philosophical zombies, and Graham Priest's dialetheism, concluding that dreams could be experiences of an objective world, with waking and dreaming on a par.
- ch. 15 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Hannah Arendt, Richard Rorty — The Banality of Evil; The Ethics of Care; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry reads Neverwhere's magic invisibility as a model of real social invisibility: after Richard helps the injured Door he loses his job, his fiancee Jessica, and even the ability to be perceived, joining the homeless, slaves, and Jews under Nazism as people excluded from the moral community whose needs no longer register. Using Arendt's banality of evil to explain everyday indifference and Richard Rorty on torturers who fail to see a 'real' human, he distinguishes radical from partial invisibility, shown in Jessica stepping over the bleeding Door and misreading her need as 'sleep it off.' The remedy is Iris Murdoch's 'loving gaze' of just and careful attention, which seizes Richard before he can rationalize, backed by a practical wisdom about whose needs matter, so that acknowledging the invisible, down to apologizing to a rat in London Below, is what makes both them and us better.
- ch. 16 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito — Kandace Lytle maps Coraline's other mother onto Descartes's evil genius: a world-manipulating deceiver whose seductive sensory pleasures, from the gravy-train dinner to the adoring other father's songs, must be doubted in favor of the intellect, exactly as the wax argument shows that understanding comes from the mind and not the senses. Because Coraline enters the portal awake, Gaiman sidesteps the dream-skepticism worry and makes the other mother's world a parallel reality built to entrance, seduce, and possess her. Coraline's refusal to sew buttons in place of her eyes protects her autonomy and free will, the ghost children who lost their names and memories show what surrender costs, and the nameless cat's 'we know who we are, so we don't need names' guides her to the cogito, so that she defeats the deceiver by finding the 'I' in Coraline, a self-sufficiency the 2009 film version, the author argues, fails to capture.
- ch. 17 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Frank Jackson, Thomas Nagel — The Knowledge Argument (Mary's Room); What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; Being-Toward-Death — Andrew Terjesen asks what Death could learn from living one mortal day per century in Sandman's Death: The High Cost of Living, after a little girl's 'How would you like it?' shamed the once icy Death into the practice. Using Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Nagel's bat to probe whether knowing what mortality is like requires first-person experience, he raises the 'Soul Man Effect' objection that Didi, like the fake black student in the 1986 film, always knows she will revert to being Death, and argues that simulation, not verbal description, is the efficient way to convey life's texture (Didi's hot-dog aftertaste). The real lesson, he concludes, is the existentialist one that each of us stands alone at death and that life's meaning lies in the unnoticed 'little moments' the dying regret missing, which only immersion in the distractions of living can teach Death, which is why the one-day-a-century program must continue.
- ch. 19 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Jean-François Lyotard — The End of Grand Narratives — Wade Newhouse reads The Graveyard Book as a fusion of the coming-of-age tale and the Gothic ghost story, from The Turn of the Screw to Stephen King's haunted narcissists, and uses Lyotard's postmodern condition to explain the hybrid: Bod's self forms not by accepting one governing metanarrative but at Lyotardian 'nodal points' among many ghosts, each a fragment of history with its own partial morality, from the Roman Caius Pompeius to the witch Liza Hempstock. The Danse Macabre, where living and dead mix under rules neither remembers choosing, dramatizes borders that feel absolute, yet Bod's development consists in violating boundaries, befriending the outcast witch and hunting the Jacks on his own terms. The ending, 'I'm Nobody Owens. That's who I am,' offers a postmodern self most itself by being no one, with the acceptance of death as the one metanarrative even postmoderns keep, for Bod it is the first lesson rather than the last.
- ch. 20 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Jacques Derrida, Michel Foucault, Jeremy Bentham — Forgiveness; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; The Panopticon (surveillance) — Najwa Al-Tabaa reads Sandman: Season of Mists through Derrida's paradox that only the unforgivable can truly be forgiven: Morpheus's freeing of Nada works as forgiveness precisely because condemning his lover to Hell was unforgivable, while Lucifer, who was never wronged by the damned, can give them only a devalued semblance of pardon, and they cling to punishment they feel they deserve. She then brings in Foucault's Discipline and Punish and Bentham's Panopticon to read the angels' rebuilt Hell of redemption as the modern rehabilitative prison, where watched souls are expected to reform themselves. The experiment fails, she argues, because redemption is imposed without hearing the prisoners, violating Derrida's condition that forgiveness needs a shared language, so the inmates prefer Lucifer's honest eternity of despair to a salvation they never asked for, a lesson about real prisons that seek rehabilitation through punishment.
- ch. 21 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Jean-Paul Sartre, Søren Kierkegaard — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Authenticity; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Wayne Yuen uses The Graveyard Book to teach the good life: Bod's family's murder, like students owing their existence to the Holocaust, is an unalloyed moral evil that still enables a better life, and Saul Smilansky's distinction between being 'sorry for' and 'sorry that' lets Bod benefit without endorsing the tragedy. His graveyard education is Aristotelian, virtues acquired through practice and models, from the Owenses' duty and Silas's wisdom to 'righteous indignation' against school bullies and friendship with Scarlett as intrinsically valuable, all building toward eudaimonia. The existentialist virtue of authenticity (attributed to Sartre and Kierkegaard) explains why Bod must be 'nobody but himself' rather than a copy of the vampire Silas, why the scavenged identities of the ghouls mark inauthenticity, and why wiping Scarlett's memory threatens her authenticity, resolving the apparent conflict between virtue and being oneself because bravery or wisdom is relative to the individual.
- ch. 22 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Eternal Recurrence; Amor Fati (love of fate); The Übermensch; The Death of God — Brandon Kempner reads Gaiman's Batman: Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader? as Nietzschean eternal recurrence: Batman dies and is reborn as the infant Bruce Wayne to repeat his life exactly, because Gaiman first strips away every teleological ending, Catwoman kills Batman, Alfred reveals he invented the Joker, and the Moore-style domestic bliss of the Superman farewell is denied. With God dead there is no Heaven, telos, or external reward, so, like Nietzsche's Overman who creates values above the city's conventional morality, Batman's meaning can lie only in the lived repetition itself: 'the only reward you get for being Batman? You get to be Batman,' the highest formula of life-affirmation. Kempner extends the pattern to the funeral-framed rebirth of a new Dream in Sandman: The Wake, showing Gaiman's recurring obsession with cycles that have 'no endings' across his work.
- ch. 24 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** David Lewis, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Bertrand Russell, Plato — Language Games — Tuomas Manninen asks how Gaiman's recycled mythological figures can be the same characters as their originals when Revelation's male, sword-wielding War becomes Good Omens' arms-dealing Carmine 'Red' Zuigiber and Pestilence retires in 1936 for Pollution, with the problem of talking truthfully about non-existent entities reaching back to Plato's Sophist. David Lewis's 'Truth in Fiction' makes the original author the arbiter of a character's properties, and Amie Thomasson's artifact theory makes fictional characters abstract artifacts created by authors, but only adding the type/token distinction and Wittgenstein's family resemblances, the same criss-crossing network of overlapping similarities by which we count games, lets Revelation's Four Horsemen and Gaiman's Four Bikers be tokens of one type. He closes with Russell's defense of philosophy's value: like Richard Mayhew's tale of London Below, a philosophical answer need not convince or be final to teach us 'what things may be.'
- ch. 25 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard, Michel Foucault — Existence Precedes Essence; Authenticity; Bad Faith; Anxiety (the dizziness of freedom) — Robert Tally Jr. reads The Graveyard Book as 'spectral existentialism': Bod's climax, 'I'm Nobody Owens. That's who I am,' is Sartre's existence precedes essence made literal, a self made rather than found, and the climactic claiming of the name enacts the self-ownership of the nursery-rhyme pauper 'who nobody owns.' Heidegger supplies the uncanny not-at-home-ness (unheimlich) of the graveyard, which Tally, citing Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces,' calls a heterotopia, while Silas the vampire embodies Lukacs's transcendental homelessness and Kierkegaardian anxiety is transmuted by Bod into the spectral gift of Fear he wields on his bullies. The identity-leeching ghouls named after the Duke of Westminster and the 33rd President are the avatars of bad faith, and the Jacks' attempt to dodge the prophecy fulfills it like Oedipus's, showing that Bod's fate, too, is self-made.
- ch. 26 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 27 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 28 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Praise" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Through a Screen Darkly" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Chapter 01 - Hollywood Doesn’t Know Dick" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Philosophical Skepticism — Ethan Mills opens his 'investigation' of Hollywood's Dick adaptations (Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, The Adjustment Bureau) by insisting that fan complaints signal something essential lost in translation from print to film, not mere infidelity. He frames the issue as a clash between two philosophical worldviews about free will and knowledge, adopting a bounty-hunter persona to hunt down what Hollywood changed.
